young.html: Thomas Aquinas was a friar and teacher who lived in Italy and France about 750 years ago. He was big, quiet and slow to speak, and some students called him "the dumb ox." His teacher, Albert the Great, is said to have answered that one day the whole world would hear this ox bellow. Thomas became one of the most famous thinkers of the Middle Ages.

His great book, the Summa Theologica, is a giant set of questions. Each one is asked like this: "Whether ...?" Then Thomas does something surprising. Before he gives his own answer, he lists the best reasons against it, as fairly as he can. Only then does he answer, and then he replies to every reason he listed.

young.name: gb-summa-article
young.cap: Press "Next part" to build an article one step at a time: the question, the objections, "On the contrary", "I answer that", and the replies.

young.html: His most famous question is "Whether God exists?" Thomas starts from things anyone can see, like a ball that rolls because a foot kicked it, and asks: what started the chain? He gives five ways of answering, which we look at in the full lesson.

Write an article like Thomas. Pick a small question, such as "Whether dogs are better pets than cats?" or "Whether bedtime should be later on weekends?" Write: (1) Objections: two good reasons for the side you disagree with. (2) On the contrary: one thing someone wise has said on your side. (3) I answer that: your answer and why. (4) Replies: a fair answer to each objection. Read it to someone. Was it hard to make the other side sound strong?
Thomas believed that faith and reason are friends. Both, he thought, come from God, so the truth found by careful thinking can never really fight the truth taught by faith.

full.html: Thomas Aquinas (c. 1225–1274) was born at Roccasecca, near Aquino, south of Rome, into a noble family. As a young man he joined the Dominicans, a new order of preaching friars. His family was so set against it that they kept him at home for about a year, but he held firm. He studied under Albert the Great in Paris and Cologne and taught at the University of Paris and in Italy.

His century was busy with new learning. Most of Aristotle's works had just been translated into Latin, with commentaries by Muslim and Jewish thinkers such as Avicenna, Averroes and Maimonides. Some Christians feared Aristotle; others followed him too far. Aquinas set out to show how the best of this philosophy could fit with Christian faith. He began the Summa Theologica ("summary of theology") around 1265, as a teaching book for beginners, and left it unfinished at his death in 1274.

The Summa has three parts: the First Part on God and creation (this rung), the Second Part on human action, happiness, virtue and law (the next two rungs), and the Third Part on Christ and the sacraments. Each part is divided into questions, and each question into articles.

full.name: gb-summa-article
full.cap: Build Article 3 of Question 2 step by step, then try the other articles from later rungs.

full.html: Every article has the same five parts: the question ("Whether ...?"); objections ("It seems that ..."), the strongest arguments for the view he will reject; "On the contrary" (Latin Sed contra), an authority on the other side; "I answer that" (Latin Respondeo), his own reasoned answer; and replies to the objections. It is the form of a university debate, written down.
Stating your opponents' arguments at full strength before answering is still a good test of an argument. If you cannot answer the best case against you, you have not finished thinking.

The Summa opens by asking whether we need any teaching beyond philosophy (Question 1). Aquinas answers yes. Some truths about God, such as that God exists, can be reached by reason, though only by a few people, after a long time and with many mistakes. Others, such as the Trinity, he holds can be known only because God has revealed them. So both are needed.

In a famous reply in the same question he says that grace does not destroy nature but perfects it. Faith, as he sees it, builds on human reason the way a teacher builds on what a student already knows.

Question 2 asks three things. Is it self-evident that God exists? Aquinas says it is self-evident in itself but not to us, because we do not know what God is; so it needs showing. (Here he answers an argument made famous by Anselm, that God is "that than which nothing greater can be thought," and does not accept it as a proof.) Can it be shown? Yes, he says, from God's effects, the way we reason from smoke to fire. Does God exist? Here come the five ways.

full.text:
The existence of God can be proved in five ways.

The first and more manifest way is the argument from motion. It is certain, and evident to our senses, that in the world some things are in motion.
full.work: Summa Theologica, First Part, Question 2, Article 3
full.author: Thomas Aquinas
full.tr: the Fathers of the English Dominican Province

full.html: "Motion" for Aquinas means any change from being able to be something to actually being it, as wood that can be hot becomes hot in a fire. Nothing, he argues, brings itself from "can be" to "is"; something already actual must do it. And the chain of movers cannot go on forever, or there would be no first mover, and so no movers after it.

full.text: Therefore it is necessary to arrive at a first mover, put in motion by no other; and this everyone understands to be God.
full.work: Summa Theologica, First Part, Question 2, Article 3
full.author: Thomas Aquinas
full.tr: the Fathers of the English Dominican Province

full.name: gb-five-ways
full.cap: Pick a way, then step back along its chain until you reach Aquinas's key premise and his conclusion.

head: Way
Starts from
Arrives at
rows: A first mover, moved by no other
Things have causes; nothing causes itself
Things come to be and pass away
A being that exists necessarily, of itself
Things are more and less good, true, noble
Something best, the cause of goodness in all
Things without minds act toward ends
An intelligent being who directs them
full.cap: The five ways, summarized in our own words.

full.text: Therefore some intelligent being exists by whom all natural things are directed to their end; and this being we call God.
full.work: Summa Theologica, First Part, Question 2, Article 3 (the fifth way)
full.author: Thomas Aquinas
full.tr: the Fathers of the English Dominican Province

full.title: The shape of the first way
full.q: Set out the first way as numbered premises and a conclusion.
steps: 1. Some things are in motion (we see it).
2. Whatever is in motion is moved by something else.
3. The chain of movers cannot go back forever.
4. So there is a first mover, moved by no other (from 1, 2 and 3).
5. This first mover is what people call God (Aquinas's closing step).
full.a: Premises 2 and 3 do the work; most later debate is about them, and about the step from 4 to 5.

full.html: Thinking the chain in the second way runs back in time, like parents and grandparents. Aquinas means causes acting at once, here and now, as a hand moves a stick that moves a stone. In fact he held (Question 46) that reason alone cannot prove the world had a beginning in time; he believed it did, on faith.

full.text: What God is, and is not

full.html: After showing that God exists, Aquinas warns that we cannot know what God is in himself, only what he is not. God is not made of parts, not changing, not limited. He calls God simple, perfect, good, infinite, everywhere, unchanging, eternal and one (Questions 3 to 11). When we use words like "good" or "wise" of God, he says (Question 13), we use them neither in exactly the same sense as of people nor in a totally different one, but by analogy: they point to something real in God that far exceeds what the words mean for us.
The first objection in Article 3 is the oldest one: if God were infinitely good, there would be no evil, but there is. Aquinas answers with Augustine.

full.text: Since God is the highest good, He would not allow any evil to exist in His works, unless His omnipotence and goodness were such as to bring good even out of evil.
full.work: Summa Theologica, First Part, Question 2, Article 3, Reply to Objection 1 (quoting Augustine)
full.author: Thomas Aquinas
full.tr: the Fathers of the English Dominican Province

full.text: Creation, angels and the human soul

items: Creation (Questions 44 to 46): God makes all things from nothing, freely, and holds them in being at every moment.
Angels (Questions 50 to 64): pure minds without bodies. Aquinas's careful treatment earned him the title "the Angelic Doctor."

The human soul (Questions 75 to 89): the soul is the "form" of the body, what makes a living human body human. Against Plato, who pictured a soul using a body, Aquinas follows Aristotle: a person is one thing, body and soul together. Yet he argues the soul can survive death, because thinking is not the act of a bodily organ.

full.html: Aquinas presents all this as reasoned teaching within his Christian faith. Readers of every belief have studied the Summa for its arguments and its method.

deep.html: Read a few articles and you meet the whole library of the Middle Ages: Aristotle, whom Aquinas calls simply "the Philosopher"; Augustine, quoted more than anyone else; Boethius; the writer called Dionysius; the Muslim philosophers Avicenna and Averroes ("the Commentator"); and the Jewish philosopher Maimonides ("Rabbi Moses"). Aquinas disagrees with many of them and still treats each with respect, as a partner in a search for truth.

Aquinas's work was argued over in his own day. Some ideas linked with him were among the propositions condemned by the bishop of Paris in 1277, and Franciscan thinkers such as Duns Scotus offered rival systems. He was declared a saint in 1323. In 1879 Pope Leo XIII urged Catholic schools to study his philosophy, and it is still taught today.

Later philosophers tested the five ways hard. David Hume (Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion, 1779) questioned whether order in nature points to one designer; Immanuel Kant (1781) argued that reasoning from the world to a first cause goes beyond what reason can know. Defenders answer that the five ways are about causes acting here and now, not a story about the past, and that Aquinas's "first" means something quite different from a first item in a series. The debate continues among philosophers today.

items: Can a chain of causes go back forever? Does it matter whether the causes act one after another or all at once?
Is it fair to call the end of each way "God"? What extra steps would you need?
Aquinas says we know more about what God is not than what God is. Can we talk sensibly about something we cannot picture?
Is stating the other side's best arguments a good habit in every disagreement?

deep.html: Later on this ladder, Dante places Aquinas among the wise in the heaven of the Sun, and Descartes, Hume and Kant take up the same questions in new ways.

questions: Why do you think Aquinas wrote out the arguments against his own view first? Would that help or hurt in a family argument?
Aquinas thought faith and reason could not truly conflict. What do you think he would do if they seemed to?
Pick one of the five ways. Explain it to someone in your own words, with an everyday example.
Is there anything you believe that you could not prove? Is there anything you could prove that others doubt?
Aquinas was called "the dumb ox" because he was quiet. Have you known someone quiet who turned out to be very wise?
